title: Dukkha and Waking Up
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The talk's main teaching emphasizes the importance of embracing uncertainty and discomfort in life, rather than trying to control or avoid it. By facing our painful experiences head-on through mindfulness practice, we can gain insight into our patterns of suffering and ultimately break free from them. This approach encourages us to cultivate a mindset of openness and awareness, allowing us to respond to life's challenges with greater authenticity and freedom.

sentences.text: Today's Dharma talk is being presented by Shudo Chris Burkhart, who is a priest with Red Cedar Zen Community.
Thank you for the introduction, and good morning.
Before I start my talk, I would like to read you a poem.
It is "The Buddha's Last Instruction" by Mary Oliver.
*Make yourself a light, said the Buddha before he died.
I think of this every morning as the East begins to tear off its many clouds of darkness, to send up the first signal, a white fan streaked with pink and violet, even green.
An old man, he lay down between two [unclear: "salad trees"].
And he might have said anything, knowing it was his final hour.*
*The light burns upward.
It thickens and settles over the fields.
Around him, the villagers gathered and stretched forward to listen.
Even before the sun itself [unclear: "hangs, this attached in the blue air"], I am touched everywhere by its ocean of yellow waves.
No doubt he thought of everything that had happened in his difficult life.
And then I feel the sun itself as it blazes over the hills like a million flowers on fire.
Clearly, I'm not needed.
Yet I feel myself turning into something of inexplicable value.
Slowly, beneath the branches, he raised his head.
He looked into the faces of that frightened crowd.*
So, good morning again, and thank you for joining us today.
I am always startled by how we think things are going to be.
Last night I wrote my talk, and I thought I would go to bed and fall asleep.
But that didn't happen until about 2 o'clock.
And then I found out later it was around 4:20 a.m.
Something went ding, ding.
And I said, "Stop, Alexa."
But it kept going ding, ding, ding, ding, ding until I yelled, "Shut up, Alexa, shut up."
And it still kept on going.
Then, in my sleep-befuddled mind, I finally realized it was the doorbell.
So my partner, Reg, and I went to the door and looked out, because where I live, you don't just open the door when the doorbell rings at 4:20 in the morning.
Outside was this fellow, shivering in the rain.
It was close to freezing.
It was really cold.
We opened the door and there was this man, no mask, barefoot, no socks, drenched, shivering.
He told us that he didn't know where he was or how he got here, and he asked for help.
I'm over 60, therefore somewhat COVID-compromised.
My partner is over 70 and has a bit of a heart condition.
So the first thing we gave him was a mask.
Then I got my favorite blanket and told him to keep it, and a towel.
Reg found some socks and some shoes.
So he had the blanket and the rain cape.
We connected with the people who would pick him up, and we kept an eye out for him and gave him something to eat and drink, something hot.
And we heard the car come, and he disappeared.
I didn't fall right asleep after that happened.
It was a really good reminder that we just don't know what's going to happen.
We have these stories about our lives, and they and reality really don't mesh too much.
So, thank you again for joining us today, and I hope you're well.
Can I see what the temperature in the room is?
Thumbs up, thumbs down or sideways?
Oh, that's all over the place.
Some are doing great.
That's fantastic.
I really hope that you're hanging in there.
And why do I hope that?
Because for me, our hanging in there together makes the hanging in there more tolerable and more acceptable and more doable.
I plan on writing these nice talks, but then current events or circumstances, life itself, looks me straight in the eye and refuses to be ignored.
When the election was over in November, I breathed a sigh of relief.
A weight dropped off our collective shoulders.
There was a bit of lightness sneaking in edgewise.
And the fact that there are several vaccines that appear to be highly effective gives hope.
Vaccinations have begun.
Some of my friends who work in the medical field have already received one or two injections.
And I am myself very much looking forward to receiving the vaccine too, because I think that the coronavirus will stay with us in the future, just like the flu.
But then there's the bad news of, I think they call it B.1.1.7, the variant in Great Britain.
That's about 50, 60 percent more infectious than COVID-19.
So I am tired after this political four-year-long roller coaster.
The events occurring in the Capitol last Wednesday, and perhaps I should say probably more of the same on the 20th during the inauguration, do trigger me.
I feel strong emotions around this.
And Joe Biden, who in the beginning at least did not look that great, he wasn't very exciting, but with time passing, he looked better and better.
Because I don't know about you, I don't want exciting right now.
I am hoping for solid and boring political stability, experience, skill.
That right now is so much better than excitement.
You may ask, why do I bring up COVID-19 and politics?
The answer is because they are there.
Because we live in this world.
It is right here all around us.
We don't avoid it.
How could we?
Times have been stressful.
It is just a mess in the Capitol, just being another event in a long series of bizarre events.
When meditating, or when I do a body scan, when we pay attention, we can probably find a white noise background of stress.
Working with this unease, this stress, is a very interesting undertaking.
At the same time, the events that cause the stress also create a vibrant sense of curiosity and discovery when we meet the unexpected, irregardless whether we like it or not.
Even if we had a magic wand to make it all disappear, we need to plumb the depths of this anxiety.
And by the way, A, we don't have a magic wand.
And B, we actually need this unease, this feeling of things being slightly off at least, because our goal is transformation.
And our awakening in the end, in large part, depends on these stumbling blocks.
If I could sing, I would sing right now, "Hello, dukkha, my old friend, I've come to talk with you again," but I'm sparing you.
So let's talk about dukkha a bit.
The automatic human response to meeting dukkha is to want to avoid that which is unpleasant, to make it go away, the faster the better.
But before we get further into it, I'd better dive into a brief definition of dukkha.
It is one of the words that give Buddhism a not so good reputation, because in English, dukkha is usually translated as suffering.
But the word suffering doesn't do dukkha justice.
It falls short.
Dukkha is much more subtle than suffering.
With suffering, we usually have a pretty good handle on whether we are actively suffering or not.
But dukkha is the fundamental unsatisfactoriness and painfulness of human life, especially the unexamined life.
Dukkha is important in Buddhism.
It is the first of the Four Noble Truths, the fact that dukkha is all around us.
And it is one of the three marks of existence.
Dukkha is sometimes translated as unhappiness, pain, suffering, unsatisfactoriness or stress.
It is the niggling feeling of dissatisfaction when we think that actually everything should be good.
Dukkha spans from boredom to hot tears, to a heart that feels so broken it will never mend again, and everything in between.
So for my fellow Buddhist geeks, here's a quick footnote on what the three marks of existence are.
They are called dukkha, anatta, and anicca.
Anicca is impermanence, meaning that all conditioned things are in a constant state of flux.
We have already mentioned dukkha, stress, suffering, and the last of the three is anatta.
Now anatta is one of the tougher Buddhist teachings.
It refers to the doctrine of non-self, that there is no unchanging permanent self.
It says there is no soul, as we know it from the Christian religion, in living beings, and that no phenomena have an abiding essence.
Now you may ask, what is all the talk about suffering?
The theme of Zen life in 2021 is awakening, enlightenment, practice, realization.
I could be flippant and repeat the teaching that being ignorant of the three marks of existence will cause us to remain in samsara and thereby prevent enlightenment.
Samsara is this world where beings are caught in repeated existences over and over again in an endless cycle.
And direct insight into the three marks brings an end to samsaric existence, and as a result, an end to suffering.
But I think presenting it like this would not be very helpful.
So I will take a different approach.
I will say it is human to avoid that which is unpleasant, and dukkha definitely qualifies as unpleasant.
The automatic response, the instinctive reaction, is to not go there.
And if we are there, to turn around and head the other way.
I think it would be fair to say that this is a shared human automatic response.
But this avoidance, this fear of discomfort, is a pitfall.
By dancing around the painful bits and pieces, we avoid the temporary pain of confronting, of dealing with it.
But there is a high cost attached to this avoidance.
Once we avoid it, we basically always have to avoid it.
And by repeating this avoidance pattern, what do we learn?
We learn avoidance, not dealing with anything.
The underlying causes of dukkha are not examined.
That spot right there: let's not go there.
Let's go around.
And it's not one spot.
I don't know about you, but if I did that, I'd be tap dancing all day.
So we do something different.
Instead of turning away, we turn towards.
Maybe we could describe Zen as never turning away, to open our eyes to whatever presents itself.
This concept has actually even worked its way into books and movies.
The iconic line from Frank Herbert's *Dune* has been an influence for the last 40 or 50 years.
*I must not fear.
Fear is the mind killer.
Fear is the little death that brings total obliteration.
I will face my fear.
I will permit it to pass over me and through me.
And when it has gone past, I will turn the inner eye to see its path.
Where the fear has gone, there will be nothing.
Only I will remain.*
Never thought I would be quoting Frank Herbert in a Dharma talk, but what can I say?
So the Buddha taught about karmic conditioning.
Karmic conditioning is the process by which a person's nature is shaped by their actions.
Every action we take influences our character for the future.
By being repeated, habits will magnify, and they will magnify both positive and negative traits just through repetition.
Another way of facing the fear, the pain, and karmic conditioning is on the cushion, through zazen.
Shohaku Okumura wrote:
*Only in zazen can we stop making karma.*
Maybe we can take it a step further and say that in zazen we can start to unravel some of our ancient twisted karma.
Some of the karma we have acquired in our lifetime.
Some of the karma we've received as a national karma, the karma of our skin color, where we were born, how we were raised.
We can quietly sit with our past, with our joy, with our pain.
In zazen, we see the arising and the passing away of our thoughts, our emotions, our likes and dislikes.
And if we hang out with all this without grasping or running away, we may even make friends with it all.
Of course, we can't stay on the cushion forever.
Sooner or later we get up and go about our life.
We have a cup of coffee, we have a meal, we engage with the news, with whatever is happening in our life.
So why do we sit in the first place if we have to get up again?
Here I am not speaking for others.
I cannot speak for your experience.
But my experience was this, just this.
Sitting zazen, I know what my life is.
When I am not paying attention and I am mindlessly going about my life, I am not in touch with this zazen mind.
One sits and one sees.
One gets up and one sees no longer, but one still has seen.
There is an art of conducting oneself in life that is informed by the memory of what one saw on the cushion.
When one can no longer see, one can still remember and still know.
And if one is fortunate, this direct encounter, this immediate experience, stays with us.
So why do I go practice?
I practice so I can come back to my regular life.
I will face my fears.
I will permit it to pass over and through me.
And when it has gone past, I will turn the inner eye to see its path, so that I can see the place I came from with new eyes and a new heart.
When I come back, when I get up from the cushion, I stand in the same place.
From the outside, it may look the same, no difference, but coming back to the place from which I started is not the same as never having left.
And off I go, making new karma.
So I will end this talk with one of my favorite poems.
It is called "Things to Think" by Robert Bly.
It is my favorite in a strange way.
The story it tells seems to be a little bit different each time, and I haven't figured it out all the way, so we are not quite done with each other yet.
So here we go.
"Things to Think" by Robert Bly.
*Think in ways you've never thought before.
If the phone rings, think of it as carrying a message larger than anything you've ever heard, [unclear: "Baster"] than a hundred lines of Yeats.

Think that someone may bring a bear to your door, may be wounded and deranged, or think that a moose has risen out of the lake and he's carrying on his antlers the child of your own, whom you've never seen.*

*When someone knocks on the door, think that he's about to give you something large, tell you that you are forgiven, or that it's not necessary to work all the time, or that it's been decided that if you lie down, no one will die.*
*Think in ways you've never thought before.
If the phone rings, think of it as carrying a message larger than anything you've ever heard, [unclear: "Baster"] than a hundred lines of Yeats.*

*Think that someone may bring a bear to your door, may be wounded and deranged, or think that a moose has risen out of the lake and he's carrying on his antlers a child of your own, whom you've never seen.

When someone knocks on the door, think that he's about to give you something large, tell you that you are forgiven, or that it's not necessary to work all the time, or that it's been decided that if you lie down, no one will die.*
Thank you so much for listening.
I hope that you carry away something from these Buddhist teachings, but if you do not connect with what I said, please absolutely forget every word and just return to your practice.
Thank you very much.
May our intention equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's words.
*Beings are numberless, I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible, I vow to end them. [unclear: "Armageddon gates"] are boundless, I vow to end them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable, I vow to become it.*
